significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish both a phenomenon and mechanism: a conserved quantity is encoded as a "linear direction that remains approximately invariant along a trajectory," and removing it harms "long-horizon rollout stability more than short-horizon accuracy." This is form (iii), combining an invariance across timesteps with an ordered causal effect across forecast horizons; it predicts behavior on unmeasured timesteps and supports an explanation of rollout drift, while work such as Greydanus et al. (2019) and Cranmer et al. (2020) shows that conservation structure can be load-bearing for learned dynamics. Verified false is distinguishable but less decisive: it would reject this linear, causally used invariant account in generic transformers, not rule out nonlinear or distributed conservation representations. In the topic-substitution check, the generic topic would support only the obvious probe-and-ablate hypothesis; the within-versus-across-trajectory invariance and long-versus-short-horizon ordering are claim-specific reasons for scoring above the topic median.

reach.justification: The claim hands over two named handles: an "invariance index" based on within- versus across-trajectory variance and an "invariant direction" that can be projected out as an intervention. These are primarily post-hoc research diagnostics rather than explicit ex-ante screens, since the claim does not state that the index forecasts failure before rollouts are attempted. After per-model re-extraction, however, the conclusion predicts a transferable qualitative relation—near-constancy along conservative trajectories, absence under broken conservation, and selectively greater long-horizon damage from ablation—across the asserted class of transformers trained on conserved dynamical systems, although uptake is mainly among dynamics and interpretability researchers rather than deployers. The topic-substitution check lowers the baseline to a generic scientific-concept probe; the reusable invariance relation and horizon-selective intervention, rather than the importance of physics itself, justify modestly above-median reach.
